project: Island ferry timetable (quality corpus: passing board) (default looks)

brief.subject: A timetable and ticket app for one island ferry line
brief.audience: daily commuters and first-time visitors, outdoors, one hand on a rail
brief.primaryJob: see the next sailing and know that it runs

categoryDefault.description: A blue brand color on a white ground, a geometric sans, and a feed of rounded cards under a map.

feedbackQuestion: For each direction and each part: keep, change or remove? Which direction is the base?

directions.name: Departure Board
directions.concept: The app is the quay-side departure board in your pocket: sailings are rows, and the next row is the biggest thing on screen.

type.source: Google Fonts. Read the license page before use

directions.imagery: No photographs. Pictograms in the style of harbour signs: one stroke weight, squared ends.
directions.texture: Flat ground. Hairline rules between rows, like the slats of a board.

layout.shape: Square corners. Full-width rows. Status sits in a boxed cell at the row end.
layout.notes: Time, pier, status. Three columns, tabular numerals.

directions.motion: A row flips once when its status changes. No easing bounce. With reduced motion the row swaps at once.
directions.signature: The next sailing as one full-width split-flap row.

sample.headline: Next boat 7:40
sample.body: On time from Pier 2. The 8:10 is cancelled for wind.

references.source: Own photo of the departure board at the quay
references.note: Row rhythm and the size of the first row.

references.license: Terms as stated on the page. Reference only
references.note: How one flap changes while the rest hold still.

directions.differsFromOthers: It reads as a public timetable in rows. B draws the whole day as one line, and C treats each trip as an object you hold.
directions.differsFromDefault: No map and no cards: one table of sailings in signage type, with the next sailing as the largest thing on screen.
directions.notes: Closest to what commuters know. Risk: it can feel like every transit board.

directions.name: Tide Line
directions.concept: The day is one horizontal line, like a tide chart: sailings are marks on it, and wind and sea state ride on the same line.

type.source: Google Fonts. Read the license page before use

directions.imagery: Drawn curves from real tide and wind data. No stock sea photographs.
directions.texture: A fine paper grain on the ground, as on a printed almanac page.

layout.shape: One long rail with round marks. Soft corners on sheets only.
layout.notes: The rail scrolls sideways. A fixed marker shows the present time.

directions.motion: The present-time marker drifts along the rail. One slow, continuous movement. With reduced motion it steps once a minute.
directions.signature: The day-long tide line with a moving marker for now.

sample.headline: Next boat 7:40
sample.body: On time from Pier 2. The 8:10 is cancelled for wind.

references.source: Scan of the printed harbour tide table, supplied by the client
references.license: Client material. Reference only, not cleared for reuse
references.note: How a curve and a table share one page.

references.license: Terms as stated on the page. Reference only
references.note: Marks on a time axis with few labels.

directions.differsFromOthers: It shows the whole day at once on a single line. A lists rows, and C stacks single trips.
directions.differsFromDefault: The timetable is a drawing, not a feed, and the weather shares the line with the sailings.
directions.notes: Best when weather decides the trip. Risk: a first-time visitor needs one line of help.

directions.name: Punched Ticket
directions.concept: The ticket is the interface: each trip is a paper ticket you hold, stamped when you buy it and punched when you ride.

type.source: Google Fonts. Read the license page before use

directions.imagery: Rubber-stamp marks and ticket-printer output. One-color line drawings of the two piers.
directions.texture: Card stock with a slight print misregistration. Perforated edges between tickets.

layout.shape: Notched ticket outlines. A round punch hole marks a used trip.
layout.notes: Ticket stack: the top ticket is the next trip. Older tickets sit below it.

directions.motion: A stamp lands on purchase: one short press. A hole appears when the trip is used. With reduced motion both appear at once.
directions.signature: The punch hole that appears in a ticket when the trip is used.

sample.headline: Next boat 7:40
sample.body: On time from Pier 2. The 8:10 is cancelled for wind.

references.source: Own photo of a punched paper ferry ticket
references.note: Notches, the punch hole and the printer type.

references.license: Terms as stated on the page. Reference only
references.note: How stamp ink sits on colored card.

directions.differsFromOthers: It makes the ticket the interface and the trip a thing you own. A and B show the service, not your trip.
directions.differsFromDefault: The ground is ticket stock, the type is printed and stamped, and the structure is a stack of tickets instead of a feed.
directions.notes: Most memorable. Risk: the timetable is one tap away, so the first screen must still answer the primary job.
